candidates.name: Private employment and manpower agency compliance pack (deposit, fee agreements, pay grids)
candidates.trigger: Décret n°2004-0054/PR/MESN, art. 3-11 (text read in the CCD legal database, which cites the Journal Officiel). Agrément from the Employment Ministry. Deposit of 4,000,000 DJF to the Treasury, revised annually to 10% of accountant-certified turnover (art. 6). Fee agreements go to the labour inspectorate (art. 9). Pay-grid agreements go to the minister (art. 8). Fees capped at 10% (placement) or 15% (temp supply) of net monthly pay (art. 10). Workers must not be charged fees (art. 7).

candidates.name: Vehicle technical-inspection scheduling and certificate register for fleet owners and inspection experts
candidates.trigger: Vehicle technical-inspection decree in the CCD 'Automobile et produits connexes' compilation (number not extracted; date unverified). Art. 1: periodic inspections at intervals of at most six months or one year depending on category. Art. 3: inspection of every imported used vehicle before registration. Art. 4: inspection before every change of owner and before the registration certificate is transferred (seller pays). Art. 6: inspections only by experts approved by the Transport Minister. Art. 8: the inspection certificate must be shown at police and gendarmerie checks.
candidates.unchecked: No competitor search run (cap reached). Whether the inspection regime is still enforced and who runs the centres (state versus private experts). Number of approved experts. Whether the inspection is digitised on the transport ministry or e-registration side. Consumer reminders alone are probably a weak business.

candidates.trigger: Loi n°202/AN/07/5e L: the company applies for an agrément to the regional state representative (art. 4). coverage.category: 2. Scrap-metal dealers
coverage.found: No dealer-licence regime found. Scrap export was suspended by a 2007 decree, with a 2013 one-company exemption (Zimmerman). In June 2021 Turkey's Corbus Metal signed an exclusivity agreement for collecting, processing and exporting all ferrous and non-ferrous scrap, including old vehicles (SteelOrbis, 28 Jun 2021). Term and current status are unverified. Little room for independent dealers to need software.

coverage.category: 3. Second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers
coverage.found: One search found no Djibouti rules on pawnbroking, brocante or friperie. Nothing new beyond the general trade licence (patente). Unverified rather than disproven.

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: No dismantler or parts-dealer regime found. Scrap and old vehicles fall under the Corbus exclusivity. Adjacent finding: used-car import is limited by vehicle age (reported 8 years, decree n°2018-203, not read). Every used import needs a technical inspection before registration, and every vehicle needs one before a change of owner (see candidate on vehicle inspection).

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: Two searches (French and English) found no Djibouti beekeeping sector, association or register. Nothing new.

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: Water Code (Loi 93/AN/95/3e L) exists, and ONEAD (Loi 145/AN/06/5e L of 2006) holds exclusive drinking-water service rights. Water is wholly groundwater from about 50 deep boreholes near the capital, mostly state-run. I could not read the drilling-permit articles. No private driller or abstractor reporting duty confirmed. Nothing new beyond the state operator model.

coverage.category: 12. Lift, boiler and pressure-equipment owners and inspectors
coverage.found: No Djibouti rule on lifts, boilers or pressure equipment found. Only foreign jurisdictions returned. Nothing new.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: Rural water points are run by village water-management committees organised under the water directorate, within the agriculture and fisheries ministry. The state in principle pays for upkeep, and the directorate lacks staff and means. A UNDP capitalisation note on participative water governance was published in Feb 2026 (not read). No statutory tariff or reporting duty found. This is donor-funded, so a software buyer is unlikely.

coverage.category: 14. Pesticide and fertiliser dealers and applicators
coverage.found: No Djibouti pesticide registration or dealer rule found. Only the WTO profile note that cattle-feed imports need Ministry of Agriculture authorisation. The agricultural sector is tiny. Nothing new.

coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: Décret n°2004-0054/PR/MESN regulates private employment agencies. They need an Employment Ministry agrément, a moral-character check, and a deposit of 4,000,000 DJF paid to the Treasury. That deposit is to be revised annually to 10% of the last accountant-certified turnover. Fees are capped at 10% of net monthly pay for placement and 15% for temp-work supply. A copy of the fee agreement goes to the labour inspectorate, and the pay-grid agreement goes to the minister. Agency count unknown. An IOM and Ministry of Labour study of recruitment practices and an ILO-supported labour-migration strategy (since 2024) are in progress. See candidate C2.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: One search returned only French material, with no Djibouti sources on funeral operators, cemetery rules or burial permits. Burial is largely religious and community-run. Nothing found.

coverage.category: 22. Grain, coffee, cocoa and other commodity traders, millers and warehouses
coverage.found: Arrêté n°2013-377/PR/MDC requires wheat flour (milled, packed or imported) to be fortified, with quality, packaging and labelling controls. A 1988 special tax on imported flour (Loi 38/AN/88/2e L) and an ONAC exemption order (n°93-0459/PRE) exist; both are old and their current force is unchecked. Cereal imports exceed 0.7 Mt a year but run through few large importers and the port, which K01/K04 cover. No stock-declaration duty found. Few buyers.

coverage.category: 23. Co-operatives, credit unions and savings groups
coverage.found: Microfinance Law n°179/AN/07/5e L (2007) puts microfinance institutions under Banque Centrale de Djibouti licensing. Associative bodies need no minimum capital but must first be declared to the oversight ministry. The Loi n°117/AN/11/6e L on financial co-operatives is on the BCD site (not read). The CPEC (Caisse Populaire d'Epargne et de Crédit) is the main body. No general co-operative law or register was found. Fishing and women's co-operatives exist, and the Ministry of Women has trained associations to become co-operatives. Buyer count is very small, and the reports are likely sent to the BCD.

coverage.category: 26. Security, cleaning and manpower agencies, and the firms that hire their workers
coverage.found: Loi n°202/AN/07/5e L (2007) governs private guarding and surveillance. It requires an administrative agrément from the regional state representative, a police inquiry, Djiboutian nationality for managers, and civil-liability insurance (art. 14). It adds a ministry agrément for the employment side. Penalties: one year in prison and a fine of 1,000,000 DJF (art. 25, partly read). Manpower agencies are under Décret 2004-0054 (see cat. 15). No cleaning-firm regime found. All of these are one-off licences rather than recurring filings. Firm counts unknown.

result.competitor: I found no Djibouti-specific AML software or service in French searches ('logiciel conformité LBC/FT Djibouti déclaration ANRF'); results were Moroccan ANRF news and generic vendors (e.g. Ease in Luxembourg, AP Solutions). Whether the ANRF uses goAML (UNODC's free reporting tool) or a custom portal is not confirmed: the goAML search returned nothing for Djibouti. If goAML is the channel, its free web form covers the filing step itself.
result.duty: Law 178/AN/25/9eme L (4 June 2025) amends AML/CFT Law 106/AN/24/9eme L. The BCD legal database dates it, and a secondary summary (regalert) says it widens obliged entities to real estate intermediaries, NGOs, VASPs and some professions and caps cash at 1,000,000 FDJ. The ANRF operational guideline (April 2026) applies it to obliged entities, non-financial professions included, and requires reports of cash, international wire and suspicious transactions. Both PDFs were compressed, so I could not read the exact articles, the NIL rule, deadlines or penalty amounts. The claim itself says non-bank obligations are 'to be specified' in later sector guidelines, so the duty may not yet be operational for DNFBPs (designated non-financial businesses and professions). The 2024 MENAFATF mutual evaluation rated most effectiveness outcomes Low; I could not open the report (403), so DNFBP supervision findings were not reached.
result.market: Not found. I found no register count of DNFBPs (real estate intermediaries, car dealers, jewellers, notaries, accountants) in Djibouti. Given the economy's size this is probably low hundreds of firms, but that is an estimate. The MENAFATF report was not reachable (403).
result.reason: The law is real. Law 178/AN/25/9eme L, which amends AML Law 106, is dated 4 June 2025 and posted on the Central Bank of Djibouti (BCD) site. A secondary summary says it adds real estate intermediaries, NGOs and other professions and caps cash payments at 1M FDJ. The ANRF guideline is dated April 2026. I could not read either PDF to confirm the cash-report, NIL and penalty clauses, and the guideline defers non-bank rules to later sector guidelines. The 2024 MENAFATF evaluation rates effectiveness mostly low, so enforcement on non-banks is doubtful. I found no local software, and the filing channel (goAML or a custom portal) is unconfirmed. The market is tiny: likely a few hundred firms, no register count found. Payment and mandatory pressure are weak today.

Two searches found no evidence of an operating periodic inspection regime in Djibouti. The only support is third-party guides saying a used-vehicle registration needs a RAD (Régie Auto de Djibouti) document issued after a technical inspection, handled via the Ministry of Equipment and Transport's Directorate of Mines and Road Safety. That suggests a single state-linked inspection tied to registration, not a recurring fleet workflow. I found no approved private experts, no count of fleet owners and no software competitor. I could not confirm the decree or enforcement. Likely few buyers, a state-run chokepoint and a weak willingness to pay, so I score it low.

decisions.reason: DNFBP buyers (dealers, brokers, notaries) with a cash-report duty to ANRF; a different buyer group and duty from K11, which covers money changers.
Data-protection duty for small firms and clinics is a new duty. Whether it is enforced is for verifiers to check.
Associations and NPOs are in scope. No recurring filing is confirmed yet, so verifiers should check.
Licensed fuel and LPG retailers with licence and return duties are a new buyer group and duty.
Fish establishments with export approval records are a new buyer group and duty, distinct from K03 and K01.
Same buyer group (livestock exporters) and same duty (Damerjog consignment dossier) as K03.
Same buyer group and same duty (monthly ITS and CNSS employer declarations) as K02.

Employment agencies have an agrément and deposit duty that is different from K02's declarations. Only the customer overlaps.
Periodic vehicle inspection for fleet owners is a new duty. No known idea covers it.
Village water committees are community bodies. No statutory duty is confirmed, so this is unverified, not out of scope.
Associative microfinance bodies reporting to the BCD are a different buyer from K11. The small buyer count is for verifiers to judge.
Flour millers and importers with fortification and quality records are a different buyer and duty from K01.
Private guarding firms with licence, insurance and contract duties are a different buyer and duty from K02.
